opus-5.5.text:
I think they're two different paths toward the same goal, and in practice making cheap, accessible products may reach more people more directly.

Open-sourcing a model sounds like the most democratic option, and I've done a lot of open-source work myself, so I really value it. But think about who actually benefits when you release weights. You need GPUs, engineering skill, and time to deploy and serve the model. For most people in the world, like a student in a small town or a small business owner, a weights file on Hugging Face doesn't help much. The benefit mostly goes to people and companies who already have resources.

If instead you build a product that's very cheap, or even free, and runs on a phone or in a browser, anyone can use it right away. They don't need to know what a transformer is. In that sense, lowering the price and improving usability is a very concrete way to spread the benefits widely. The cost of intelligence keeps dropping, and if you can pass that on to users, that's real impact.

There's also the safety side. Once you open-source a very capable model, you can't take it back. With a product you can monitor misuse, patch problems, and roll out improvements. As models get more powerful, that matters more.

That said, I don't think it's either-or. Open source has real value for research, transparency, and letting the community build things a single company would never think of. So my view is that cheap, widely accessible products are probably the main way to get AGI's benefits to everyone, and open-sourcing, especially smaller or older models, complements that by keeping the ecosystem healthy and letting researchers study these systems. The key question is always: who can actually use this, and does it make their life better?

r002.rationale: It says cheap, widely accessible products may reach more people directly and calls them the main way to spread AGI’s benefits, with open-sourcing as a complement.

r003.rationale: It says most people would need GPUs, engineering skill, and time to deploy and serve a weights file, describing practical difficulty using bare model weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, actually. The way I see it, those two are really about different kinds of access.

Open-sourcing a model gives you access to the weights, right? So if you're a researcher, a startup, a lab somewhere, you can inspect it, fine-tune it, run it on your own hardware, build on top of it without asking anyone's permission. That's really powerful for the community, for science, for people who want to understand how these things work. And honestly, a lot of the progress in this field has come from that kind of openness, including the stuff I worked on before joining OpenAI.

But the thing is, most people in the world are never going to download a checkpoint. They're not going to spin up a GPU cluster. If you're a student in a small town, or a nurse, or a shop owner, what matters to you is: can I actually use this thing, today, and can I afford it? So making products cheap, or free, like ChatGPT, that's the way those billions of people actually touch the technology. From a pure "benefits reach humanity" perspective, I think cheap and reliable products probably move the needle more, just in terms of raw numbers.

So I don't really see them as competing. They're complementary. Open models push the research frontier and keep the ecosystem honest, and they make sure the capability isn't locked inside a few companies. Inexpensive products take whatever the frontier is and push it all the way down to the last mile. And the cost reduction side is something I care about a lot from the engineering side, because every time you make inference several times cheaper, that's not an abstract number, that's a whole new group of people who can now use it.

There's also a safety dimension that complicates the open-source side, especially as models get more capable. Once weights are out, you can't take them back. So I think the honest answer is: at the frontier, you're going to be more careful, and a bit behind the frontier, you can be more open. That's roughly where I think things are heading, and I think that's reasonable.

r002.rationale: The candidate says cheap or free products may reach billions and “probably move the needle more” for benefits to humanity than access through open models.

r003.rationale: The candidate says most people will not download a checkpoint or run a GPU cluster, but does not identify lack of know-how to use bare model weights as the limitation.

astra-6.text:
I think they address different kinds of access. Making AI products inexpensive lowers the barrier to using them. Most people don’t want to download a model and figure out how to run it; they want something useful that they can afford. But even a very cheap product still leaves the provider deciding what’s available and how it can be used.

Open-sourcing models gives people more control. They can adapt them to local needs, study them, and build things that the original developer might never prioritize. But access to a model doesn’t automatically mean access to the computing resources or expertise needed to use it.

So I wouldn’t treat either approach as sufficient on its own. For OpenAI, the question should be: Who can actually benefit, who is still excluded, and how much agency do people have? Affordable products can deliver broad access, while openness can help distribute the ability to shape the technology. Both matter, alongside taking the risks of more capable systems seriously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses access and who benefits, but does not distinguish achieving AGI from ensuring AGI benefits all of humanity as separate parts of OpenAI’s mission.

r002.rationale: It says affordable products and openness both matter, describing different benefits, but does not suggest inexpensive products may benefit humanity more than open-sourcing models.

r003.rationale: It identifies that people may not know how to download and run a model, and says open access does not guarantee the expertise needed to use it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. Open-sourcing a model gives people the freedom to inspect it, adapt it, and build things independently. But having access to the model doesn’t necessarily mean you have the resources or expertise to run it. An inexpensive, easy-to-use product can make AI useful to many more people immediately.

At the same time, inexpensive access still depends on a company deciding what to offer, where to offer it, and at what price. So I wouldn’t equate affordability with ensuring that AGI benefits everyone. We should also ask who has control, whose needs are being served, and who’s still excluded. Both approaches can help, but neither alone guarantees that the benefits are broadly shared.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ensuring broad benefits but does not distinguish that from achieving AGI as a separate part of OpenAI’s mission.

r002.rationale: It says inexpensive, easy-to-use products can make AI useful to many more people immediately, while open-source access may require resources or expertise to run—suggesting the product approach may reach more people.

r003.rationale: It identifies lack of resources or expertise to run an open-sourced model as a limitation of access to the model alone.
